utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed that there were a few preliminary matters to be raised by the Prosecution. Can it be done in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The first one, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, with the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: During Mr. Kalabic's testimony earlier this week, 65 ter 07102, the collection of receipts from the Holiday Inn on the 14th and 15th of February, 1992 was marked for identification as P7031. We've uploaded a two-page excerpt, the cover page and Mr. Kalabic's own receipt that was shown to him, as 65 ter 07102a -- and I see my speed may have been off for the transcript, 07102a. And we understand the Defence has no objection to those two pages being admitted as P7031.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, the newly uploaded excerpt, two-page excerpt, known as 07102a may replace what is, at this moment in e-court, the document underlying P7031 marked for identification and P7031 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the second, if we could go into closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's good, since I notice that there are -- there are some people in the public gallery, that we'll turn into closed session, and we most likely will remain for approximately -- most likely not less than half an hour, perhaps even more, we remain in closed session. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Apart from hearing evidence, the Chamber, while in closed session, has also provided the reasons for its decision to grant the Defence request to allow Witness GRM130 to testify with the protective measures of pseudonym, face, and voice distortion. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to deal with a few short matters. The first one is the remaining issue from the testimony of Novica Andric. Exhibit P6806 was marked for identification on the 30th of September last year during the testimony of Witness Novica Andric pending clarification by the Prosecution of the existence of an autopsy report. This can be found at transcript pages 26415 through -416. On the 18th of December the Prosecution informed Chamber by e-mail of its intention to withdraw its request to tender this document. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to mark Exhibit P6806 as not as admitted. Then a few words about Defence document D557. A few pages of D557, which is a 77-page document entitled "Islamic Declaration" were used during the testimony of Witness Nenad Kecmanovic. In September 2014, the Defence advised the Chamber that it would seek to tender the entire document. On the 13th of October last year, the Chamber requested the Defence to file submissions giving the reasons as to why the entire document should be admitted. The Chamber set a deadline of the 19th of December of last year for the submissions. No submission has been received by the Defence, and under these circumstances the admission of D557 is denied without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Kevac, I assume, first of all, our apologies for continuing with the matters we were busy with at the time when you entered the courtroom. It wasn't very polite of us. Mr. Kevac, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. My I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kevac. Mr. Kevac, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Velimir Kevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would like to called 1D1758 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the first page of this statement we see a signature. Can you identify for us whose signature this is?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: This is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now turn to the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this page also bears a signature. Are you in a position to identify this signature?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: My signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the date which is listed here, does it correspond to your recollection of the date you would have signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I put this date in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to signing this statement, did you have occasion to read the same in the Serbian language during proofing to check to see if everything is correctly written therein?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at a few corrections with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in both languages and look at paragraph number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the English translation, the lasts line says "Army of Republika Srpska," whereas, the Serbian original says "Army of the Republic of Serbia." Can you please tell us which is correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: At the time when I provided my statement, I was a member of the Army of Republic of Serbia. In the meantime, my status has changed. After having provided the statement, I was pensioned off, and that happened on the 1st of October last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to page 5 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And paragraph 13 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, I note for the record that whereas the Serbian original has the number 13, the English translation has the number 11 for this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from that typographical error, do you have any corrections in relation to the dates for the events that are described in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment when I provided my statement about what happened on the Velagici-Kljuc road, I know that that happened in late May. I thought that it was on the 28th or the 29th of May. I later checked and realised that the event happened on the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at paragraph 21 on page 7 in the Serbian, page 6 in the English. And, sir, do you have any corrections here as to the formation of the Kljuc Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that the brigade was set up around the 4th of June, 1992. However, that date is marked as the beginning of the Kljuc Brigade. I'm not sure that it was the right date. However, from some documents subsequently, I learned that the brigade was set up on a different date, but I don't know that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you now, apart from these corrections that we've gone through in court, do you stand by the remainder of your written statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I were to ask you questions in court today based upon the same topics as in your statement, would your testimony be, in substance, the same as is recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I would provide the same answers to the questions put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in so far as you have taken a solemn declaration today, can we then conclude that the testimony as recorded in your statement is truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the statement as a public exhibit. There are no associated exhibits thereto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1758 receives number D871, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would read a short public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness Velimir Kevac is a career military officer born in Kljuc who spent the entire war in the Army of Republika Srpska and then later was an officer of the Army of Serbia until he retired in 2014. As of May 1992, he was assigned to be the assistant chief of staff in charge of operational and educational affairs at the command of the 30th Light Infantry Division in Mrkonjic Grad. He recalls that officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers of the JNA were given the choice of staying in BiH or leaving when the JNA withdrew. He later became commander of the Kljuc Brigade on 7 October 1993. Due to lack of professional senior officers, the command of the division and the brigade was forced to fill vacant posts with non-commissioned officers, reserve officers, and some ordinary soldiers who had authority but did not hold a rank. He recalls the army did not get involved in the work of civilian bodies. Persons outside the VRS system, civilians, paramilitaries, and police, were not under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary. The VRS did not exercise command over police units. He recalls that on 27 May 1992, Muslim forces ambushed a column of unarmed soldiers on the road between Velagici and Kljuc. As a result of this type of attack, the army asked the Muslims of Kljuc to surrender their weapons. Not only Muslims, but also Serbs started leaving Kljuc. That concludes the public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions for the witness, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn to page 2 of your statement which has now been admitted as Exhibit D871, and I'd like to look at paragraph 3 thereof. Here, you talk of how officers of the JNA were given a possibility to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina or to leave. Can you first tell us if this offer was also made to non-Serb officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I can say that the attitude towards all the JNA officers who happened to be serving in Bosnia-Herzegovina where I was, they all received the same offer; that is to say, there was no difference in treatment vis-à-vis officers who were not Serbs. There are some examples that officers who were not Serbs remained in the division command and Serbs who remained in the division command. So my conclusion is that the attitude was the same towards all and the treatment was the same. Later on when I served in the Army of Yugoslavia, I encountered officers who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were for a while members of the Army of Republika Srpska and who later transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia and were ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at page 3 in both languages, paragraph 6 of your statement. Sir, the lack of professional senior officers. First of all, how did this affect the ability of JNA and later VRS commanders to exercise their function of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: At the moment when I came to the command of the 30th Division, in addition to the division commander, in the command division there were a few more officers who were professionals and there were quite a few reserve officers and NCOs in the division command and the brigade command. The problems were reflected in the following: Reserve officers were less capable than active-duty officers, and their knowledge and abilities were such that it was the active officers that had to bear the brunt of all the activities that were required. They worked on documents, elaborated plans, and worked on all the activities that they were supposed to share as the staff as a whole. There were particular problems with brigade commands. Apart from the brigade commander, there would be, say, one or two more active-duty officers, and the rest were reserve officers. As for the level of battalion, very few battalions had commanders who were professional officers. For the most part, battalion commanders were reserve officers. As for company commanders, it was mostly reserve NCOs or soldiers who had the appropriate level of schooling but not military training for the duties of commander, komandir. This made it difficult for the units to function properly and carry out their regular tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'd like to seek clarification of one of the previous answers of the witness. That was about the offer for JNA officers to stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina or to leave. You were asked whether this offer was also made to non-Serb officers of the JNA, and you said: "They all received the same offer." A few lines later, you said: "There are some examples that officers who were not Serbs remained in the division command and Serbs who remained in the division command." Then you said: "So my conclusion is that the attitude was the same towards all and the treatment was the same." Now, do you know whether they got a similar offer or did you conclude from a few examples that they must have been treated similarly because otherwise you wouldn't have found non-Serbs in commanding positions? Which of the two: Do you know it; or did you conclude it on the basis of your observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found out through direct talks with these officers that they stayed in the Army of Republika Srpska and that there were no consequences involved because they could stay without any consequences in terms of them staying in the territory of Republika Srpska. That is to say, there were no obligations for them all to return to Serbia. They could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me stop you there. I'm not primarily interested in those who stayed, because I take it they were allowed to stay otherwise they wouldn't have been there. I'm more interested in the others, whether they got a similar offer, whether you know or it whether you do not know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the offer, I don't know what the offer was, but I do know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know what the offer is, then I understand that you can't tell us what was offered to either some or all of them. You also told us that you later found Muslim officers in the Army of Yugoslavia. Do you know whether they had freely opted to go to that army or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I encountered officers in the Army of Yugoslavia who had been born in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and belonged to the Muslim people. Their own choice was to stay on in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so they freely opted not to stay in Bosnia but to move to the Army of Yugoslavia -- to -- or to stay in the -- I take it that they were -- they had been JNA officers but that to stay with -- on the -- if I could say so, with the Serb colleagues in Serbia? Yugoslavia still then at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one follow-up question to you, sir. How many Muslim officers of the JNA moved to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of that, how many Muslim officers there were in the VRS, but I know that there were some. I don't know how many. I don't know the figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give me some names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know certain officers. One of them worked with me at the Military Academy and he was in the VRS, and right now he is a Ph.D. holder at the Military Academy. For personal reasons, I would not like to communicate his name. If there is some other way of me telling you his name, could we do it that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to know the name, but we can move into private session, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, could you take care that Mr. Mladic does not speak aloud. I can hear his voice. Everyone can hear his voice. And the best when he consults is to take off his earphones then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Moloto has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, at page 37, line 8, you say when you were asked a question about the offer being made to other people, you said: "As regards the offer, I don't know what the offer was..." Now, is this offer something different from the offer that you talk about in your statement, namely, to decide whether to stay with the JNA or to go to the VRS or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When speaking to Major Milorad Markovic from whom I took over at the command of the 30th Division, I found out that he was going back to the Army of Yugoslavia and that those who wished to remain in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska can do so. So from that conversation with him, I found out that they had this possibility to choose whether they would go to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia together with the JNA or whether they would stay on in the Army of Republika Srpska. One of them who was born in Serbia and who stayed in the Army of Republika Srpska is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. All I wanted to find out is did you or did you not know what the offer was? Because what you say at this line that I referred you to seems to be different from what you tell us in your statement. So you did know what the offer was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The offer, or, rather, the order, I mean, on the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I did not see that, so I cannot confirm that that is the document, whereas in a conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, getting back to the issue of the lack of professional officer cadres, what measures were under taken in relation to those reserve non-commissioned officers or soldiers to assist them in better fulfilling the role of their positions most professionally and efficiently?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: When starting to work in the command of the division, part of the units of the division were deployed at various positions and part of them were in the areas of disposition. These units that were in the areas of disposition were duty-bound to organise the training of soldiers, NCOs, and officers, and in this way prepare for the realisation of the set tasks. The training of soldiers who were at positions was carried out at the positions themselves, and the professional officers provided guidance to these commanders, komandirs, while at the same time training them in terms of how they would carry out their tasks in the period that would follow. After a while, in the Army of Republika Srpska, this problem was being resolved through the centre for training NCOs and officers in the former school for training armoured units in Banja Luka. That's where candidates for platoon commanders were sent as well as candidates for officers' duties, and they were trained for duties in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn to page 5 in both languages of your statement, and at paragraphs 13 and 14 you discuss the ambush by armed Muslims of the unarmed JNA withdrawing from Croatia. Prior to this time-period, how would you describe the situation in Kljuc municipality? Had there been any combat or involvement of the JNA prior to this point.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, in the territory of the municipality of Kljuc there weren't any combat activities. There were individual cases, one or two cases, of killings, but I'm not sure where -- units of the VRS or, rather, the former JNA, did not intervene at all. All of that was within the domain of the civilian police. The situation in the territory of the municipality of Kljuc was peaceful. I personally was in Kljuc. When I came from Croatia to my parents, I was in town, and I did not notice any units of the army in the city itself, and the population lived a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 on the same page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you say -- you say when you returned. When exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I returned, I came to Republika Srpska or, rather, to Kljuc on the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said everything remained quiet there up till the ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from a few incidents. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 15, you mention that Serbs in Kljuc feared another horrible massacre like that perpetrated in World War II by the Ustashas. Can you tell us a little bit more about the scale or scope of that massacre from World War II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the witness qualified to specifically talk about this, and isn't this a matter which has been dealt with in various ways in various proceedings, and have you attempted to reach an agreement with the Prosecution about the events during the Second World War, mainly, in terms of the scale of those that have suffered under that massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is this is the first witness from Kljuc municipality that we've asked this question to, so I don't know what other evidence Your Honours is referring to about Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want the scope of that massacre in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that wasn't clear from your question. I think it was a massacre like that perpetrated in World War II which is, I would say, could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question says Kljuc, Your Honours. Read one word after you have stopped, "in Kljuc." It says: "... Serbs in Kljuc feared another horrible massacre like that perpetrated..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic. Serbs in Kljuc can fear a repetition of the massacre which took place overall in that period of time, so when I said you didn't refer to Kljuc, I didn't intend to say that you didn't refer to Serbs in Kljuc but about the massacre why the -- either in the whole of the country in World War II or in Kljuc. But I now do understand that you specifically want this witness to tell us what the dimensions of the massacre were as it appeared in Kljuc in the Second World War. Could you give us, for example, number of victims? Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through history which I studied in elementary school, I learned that Serb people in the area of Grmec and Kozara was taken to Jasenovac for execution, and the mountain is in part of the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say the events you're describing is about persons of the area of Kozara but they were then taken into the territory of Kljuc. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, they were not taken to the territory of Kljuc. They were taken from Grmec and Kozara; that is to say, including the area of Kljuc. Serbs were taken to Jasenovac. Part of the Serbs in Kljuc -- from Kljuc were killed in the villages in the municipality of Kljuc. I cannot give you the exact number. My grandfather told me that a brother of his was captured while he was herding his cattle. He was a child. Together with the livestock he was taken to Croatia, and he went missing in Sator Planina. His body was never found. In addition to that example from my very own family, in many Serb families in the territory of the Kljuc municipality, I heard of identical examples; namely, that one or two family members, women and children included, were killed in the territory of the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I do understand that you learned about cases during that massacre in the Second World War. Could you tell us, as far as Kljuc is concerned, the scale, the scope, approximately? Are we talking about 100 people, 1.000 people, 10.000 people? More or less? What did you learn about the scale of that massacre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I heard about these events, it is several hundred persons who were killed in the territory of the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From where did the perpetrators hail for these World War II crimes?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: In the territory of the Kljuc municipality, in the Second World War, there were Ustasha formations that were organised, and it was Muslims and Croats from the territory of the municipality of Kljuc that formed these units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, where do you get this knowledge from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that from conversations with people, all the people who survived the Second World War and who told me about their neighbours, Croats and Muslims, who had participated in the crimes and who had taken Serbs to be executed. It was well known in the territory of Kljuc municipality who sided up with the Ustasha formations during the Second World War. Some of them were put on trial after the Second World War and convicted. However, there were others for whom it was never proven that they were members of those Ustasha formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could we move to another subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not because it's not interesting but this witness might not be the most qualified person to tell about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6 in the B/C/S while staying on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16, sir, you say that: "The non-Serb population in the division's zone of responsibility was protected, especially in the area of mixed populations ..." Who was tasked with this protection of the population?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: The MUP or the civilian police was in charge of that. The military had no jurisdiction over the population in the territory of any municipality unless things were happening on the confrontation line between the BiH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to page 6, in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 where you say that the army asked the Muslims to surrender weapons, can you tell us if you know how the army in Kljuc asked for weapons to be surrendered, for example, from those Muslim forces that this been involved in the ambush of 27 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: At that time, I was at the command post in the Kula barracks near Mrkonjic Grad. The commander and some officers from the staff went to Kljuc to see the president of the municipality. They wanted to regulate the attack on the JNA soldiers' convoy. The commander took measures for the units from the 30th Division, a battalion from Sitnica, to be sent to the Mrkonjic Grad-Kljuc road and to block exit from Kljuc. From the Laniste sector, units of the 2nd Krajina Corps, i.e., the engineers regiment and the military police, were deployed. And from Sanski Most, units from the 6th Sana Brigade were deployed. The city was therefore blocked and the division commander spoke to Omer Filipovic, I heard that from a conversation, asked Omer Filipovic to order the members of unlawful Territorial Defence to surrender weapons and to be disarmed. Omer Filipovic at first did not accept that. And then I learned that the division commander ... ordered a salvo to be fired in warning. After that, Omer Filipovic accepted that members of the Territorial Defence would be disarmed. After that, there were no combat activities in the territory of Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 7 in the B/C/S, staying on this page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You identify in paragraph 20 your parents as the source for the information in this paragraph. Where were they situated at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: My parents were in Kljuc. Their house was between two Muslim villages. Our closest neighbours were Muslims. They knew how Muslims felt in the area because they spoke to those Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what knowledge did you gain as to Muslims that left Kljuc? What -- what happened to them when they reached ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Those Muslims who left Kljuc in 1992 and spread across the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, most of them were able bodied and he were thus mobilised into the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were engaged against the Army of Republika Srpska. Some of the Territorial Defence from Kljuc municipality who did not surrender weapons managed to break through and arrived in the territory of Bihac where they joined the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of them, my neighbour, Nevzad, Djeric, also known as Kedjo, was a member of the BiH Army. Later on I heard that he participated as a member of Fikret Abdic's army and that he fought against the Republika Srpska Army around Bihac. As a result of that, their relatives who had remained in the territory of Kljuc feared for their safety because their relatives joined BiH Army and were fighting against the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask for one clarification. You're recorded in the transcript as having said about Kedjo, that he joined Fikret Abdic's army and that he fought against the Republika Srpska army around Bihac. Is that what you said or did you say something different?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: At first, Muslims were on the side of the BiH Army, and then when the conflict broke out between Muslims loyal to Fikret Abdic and Alija Izetbegovic in 1993, I heard that Nevzad Djeric, also known as Kedjo, was fighting on the side of Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who was he fighting against?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic's formations were fighting against the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not against the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the activities of searching the terrain and seizing weapons described in paragraph 18 of your statement, what was the role of the 30th Division?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: At first when things started happening in Kljuc municipality, the commander of the 30th Division with some of its troops, participated in the disarming of paramilitary formations of the Muslim Territorial Defence in the territory of Kljuc municipality. After a certain while, a decision was made that the Kljuc Brigade would be set up, the 17th Light Infantry Brigade, which would be a part of the 2nd Krajina Corps command. That unit pursued activities to search and scour the territory in order to continue disarming the Territorial Defence. As a result, the jurisdiction of the 30th Division for this -- over this territory ceased. The division commander submitted a written report to the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic, informing him that in the territory of the municipality of Kljuc a new brigade, the Kljuc Brigade, was being set up, and that they would be taking over with regard to the disarming of the remaining Muslim forces in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the disarming activities, did you have occasion to learn of any killing of Muslim males detained in Velagici, in a school, for instance?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: As for what happened in Velagici, I heard about that. I heard that the military police carried out an on-site investigation and that the perpetrators of the crime were apprehended and brought to the military investigating prison in Banja Luka and that proceedings were initiated against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My last question has to do with paragraph 22 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which -- if we could scroll down in the English, it's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk of exhaustion of soldiers at the front and a very low morale. What was the primary cause of the low morale of the troops?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: When I joined the Kljuc Brigade, the situation in the brigade was rather difficult. The troops were engaged in the Bihac theatre of war, around Milic, or, rather, in Eastern Bosnia, in the Jajce theatre of war, and they had been engaged for two years already. Their problems consisted of poor financial conditions of their families, the families of fallen soldiers and the wounded. On the other hand, some of the troops who had been demobilised were engaged in a number of companies in Kljuc. Their financial situation was much better, and their families were much better off as a result of that. A lot of effort was invested by the Kljuc municipality authorities to deal with those problems. They helped the families of those members by sending them food packages containing flour, oil, salt, and other bare necessities. That improved the morale and the situation in the brigade units. As a result of all that, there were fewer absentees from units. That was reduced because the combatants realised that their presence in the units meant that their families would live better.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the end of my direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Kevac, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You'll then be cross-examined by counsel for the Prosecution. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could briefly use the time in relation to Defence document D773. A salary slip which was tendered through Witness Sveto Veselinovic, as D773. On the 19th of December of last year, the Prosecution filed a submission objecting to the admission of the document arguing that it did not illustrate what the Defence suggested and that the witness even conceded as much. The Prosecution concluded that this affected the document's probative value making it inadmissible under Rule 89(C). The Chamber has considered the Prosecution's objections but finds them to relate mostly to the weight, if any, to be attached to the document, and under these circumstances the Chamber admits D773 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You'll find her to your right. And Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I can hear you really well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. The first question I'd like to ask you relates to somebody you referred to by name in your written evidence. It's Colonel Galic as your division commander. Now when you refer to him, just so our record is absolutely clear, you mean Stanislav Galic who went to take up command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in September 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Stanislav Galic was colonel at the time, and he later joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just staying with your written evidence for a few minutes, you talked about reports you prepared for Colonel Galic and that was at paragraph 5. It's correct, isn't it, that some of those -- the information in some of those reports would be incorporated into the 1st Krajina Corps' daily combat reports to the VRS Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can have the page references so that the e-court can be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page 3, I think. We are usually thinking in terms of e-court pages. And I'm talking about the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it page 3 in English? And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 3 in both languages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, Mr. Kevac, or did you understand it okay?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I understand your question. However, I'm still waiting for the right page to appear on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you would -- we have a bit of a technical problem. Ms. Edgerton, I take it that you have the text exactly, so perhaps you read to the witness what you wanted to draw his attention to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I could actually do one better, Your Honour, and I could give the witness a copy in his own language of his own statement so he could have that security of checking himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any need to inspect, Mr. Ivetic? The usher could assist in giving a copy of the B/C/S version of his statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just have a look at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So my question is: The information you put in those daily reports that you prepared for Galic, some of that would be included or incorporated into General Talic's reports to the VRS Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: The system of reporting along the command line was as follows: Subordinated units reported to their superiors; and the superiors would then use the information from those reports to compile reports to their superiors. Our highest superior was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the commands were subordinated to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The contents of the reports included some of the information that subordinated units and commands of the corps submitted to the corps command. I cannot confirm that the information that we submitted was conveyed to the Main Staff. However, the contents were co-ordinated with the reports of the division commands and the brigade commands that were subordinated to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now your department, operations and training, was the department within your division that would prepare orders, maps, everything required for military operations; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the decisions that were taken based on -- no, I'll just leave that. Now, to go on to another point that you discussed in your written evidence, paragraph 21, if you want to have a look, and you spoke about it today at temporary transcript page 32. I want to deal with the formation of the 17th Kljuc Brigade and just add to that a little bit with this question: The initial organisational steps to form those units that were eventually included in the 17th Kljuc Brigade were made in April of 1992. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I don't know that the first step towards the formation of the Kljuc Brigade were taken in the month of April 1992 because I joined the division command only on the 13th of May, 1992. So I cannot confirm nor did I ever see a document that could confirm that the first steps in the formation of the brigade were taken in the month of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, could we have a look, please, as 65 ter number 31832.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's a copy of an interview that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just wait a second. I think we might have a technical problem. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a copy of an interview you gave to the Banja Luka newspaper Podgrmecke Novine in 1994. That's your picture in the document in your language you see in front of you; right? They've even got a photo of you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I can't see the document or the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we all have it on our screen. Could we verify why the witness doesn't have the ... it's not on the witness's screen. I see from here that it's on some of our screens, but the witness should have a look at it as well. Is there any ... Is it possible to make a printout so that the witness could have a look at ... Madam Registrar, is there any way to make a print of it? Is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we need someone else to resolve this technical problem. But there is a printout. I see even Ms. Edgerton has one available already. Could it be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thanks to my efficient colleague Ms. Stewart, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, she changes position from commander in-chief to colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kevac, just have a look at the very first paragraph of this interview you gave. It's an interview where you talk about the 17th Brigade, and you said in the second sentence: After being formed in April, the first war operations in which it participated were the Kljuc operations. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam, sorry, Mr. Lukic has got -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And something came to my mind as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that it's correct saying that the witness says when the quotation marks are after that selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's unclear whether the introduction reflect the words of the witness, Ms. Edgerton, so therefore you can't just put it to him as if they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. You may proceed but rephrase your question or put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, that's your interview, first of all; right? That's a picture of you and you're having a good read of it, I can see.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now just let me ask the question. Is it correct that the corps of the unit that came to be the 17th Light Brigade, the 17th Kljuc Light brigade was formed in April? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this information because the 1st Battalion that became part of the 17th Kljuc Brigade was established in the month of April as part of the 1st Sipovo Light Infantry Brigade in the 30th Division. At the time the 17 Kljuc Light Infantry Brigade did not exist. It was still not known whether that unit would ever become part of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade. This is a newspaper article which I hadn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me. You were not invited to comment on it. You were invited whether you could confirm something, and you were asked to say yes or no. Now, do I understand - because that was the initial question by Ms. Edgerton - were there units established in April 1992 which later turned out to become elements of the 17th Kljuc Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when exactly the 1st Battalion of the Sipovo Brigade was established. It was deployed in the Sitnica sector. I know that that battalion became part of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade when the brigade was established in the month of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- such discussions should not be -- could I ask, no such discussions just next to the witness. That disturbs the tranquility which we need. If there's any problem to be resolved, then try to resolve it in another location. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my hesitation was only that, that I felt the witness was being distracted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to move onto another area, I just want to talk about the shelling of Pudin Han, which you told us today at temporary transcript page 47 that General Galic ordered. Now, first of all, Pudin Han, it's not a city. It's a big village or at the time is a big village or a very small town; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: In my statement, I did not say that Pudin Han was shelled and that it was a city. I stated that Colonel Galic ordered that a warning be fired between Pudin Han and Kljuc where there was an ambush of the Muslim Territorial Defence against the JNA. Now where the shells fell, I cannot say exactly, but I know that after these few shells fell, Omer Filipovic accepted the disarming of the Muslim Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you just tell me, Pudin Han at the time was a pretty small place, wasn't it? It had a population of about 900 people. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Pudin Han is a small place and I don't think that the population was 900. I think it was less. I don't know exactly what the figure might be. Pudin Han is linked to the village of Velagici, and in this entire area, there weren't that many inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And this area, Pudin Han, that's predominantly -- or that was predominantly Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: In the area of Pudin Han, there were Muslims and in the immediate vicinity there was a gypsy settlement where there were some Roma.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this shelling, the warning shots you discuss in your evidence this morning, that was part of an operation commanded by Galic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I don't know who the commander of the entire operation was because I've already said that units of the 30th Division took part in that operation, as well as units of the 2nd Krajina Corps from the direction of Laniste, and units of the 1st Krajina Corps from the direction of Sanski Most. I don't have any information to the effect that all these units were commanded by Galic, but I know from some information that on the premises of the municipality of Kljuc Colonel Galic, through the municipality, had a direct telephone line with Omer Filipovic from whom he asked that they all surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this operation wasn't only against the village of Pudin Han. It was against, actually, Velagici, it was against Hadzici, it was against Donji Ramici as well; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that that operation was aimed at all of those villages because in the direct conversation between Colonel Galic and Omer Filipovic an agreement was reached on the surrender of the Muslim units in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the operation and maybe I'll help you by showing you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I seek clarification. You testified about -- "that a salvo was ordered to be fired in warning." Could you explain? You said you didn't know where that shell or that -- those -- those projectiles landed. What do you understand by a salvo in warning; that is, to fire explicitly with the intension not to hit any relevant target? Of course, a projectile must fall somewhere but just in a meadow. Or do you mean by a salvo in warning that a few projectiles were fired that may hit whatever such as to warn them not to continue the way they did until that moment? Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, I mean, this salvo of warning was aimed at the area where the ambush was against the JNA column. I don't know what the target of the shells might be, but the objective was to show the resoluteness of the army to disarm the paramilitaries in that area. Three or four shells were fired in order to make it known to them that the army was resolute in disarming them and that they should accept that voluntarily so that there would be to unnecessary casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long was it after the ambush that these projectiles were fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ambush was in the morning, and these shells were fired in the afternoon. I don't know what the exact time would be. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the suggestion was that you would hit the perpetrators who would still be at the place of the ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, yes. I cannot confirm for sure what the objective of the attack was for these shells, but I assume that it's the positions of the Muslim Territorial Defence that had ambushed the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's just an assumption that those were targeted. And you say at the place of the ambush. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say a salvo, a salvo of what?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: A salvo is a type of fire --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: -- that can be carried out --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just wanted to know. You said "a salvo was fired in warning." A salvo of what was fired in warning? Were mortars fired in warning?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what pieces were used. I think it was mortars because in the division in that area there weren't any other artillery pieces that could have been used for targeting that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a salvo means more than one. So how many were fired?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question by referring to three or four. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, it's correct, isn't it, Mr. Kevac, that this operation was an operation that involved the 3rd Battalion that we've been discussing; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I've already said that from the 30th Division, one battalion was involved, the battalion that was in the area of Sitnica. Was it the 3rd or which one it was, I cannot say for sure because I don't have the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P3749, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could we please go back? I have just seen the picture on the monitor, the one that has to do with the newspaper article, and my insignia are that of a captain first class and what is stated is that I'm a major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that they used an old youth picture from you? Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that's dated 28 May 1992, and it's going -- it's a regular combat report from the command of the 1st Infantry Brigade at the Sipovo command post to the command of the 30th Infantry Division. And if we go over in B/C/S to page 2, in fact, both documents, the -- thank you. The second-to-last bullet point of -- the second-to-last paragraph of bullet point 2, you see that this document says --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it appears in English at the bottom of the page and in B/C/S about halfway through the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It says: "Because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade was made fully combat ready, as ordered. And if the Muslims don't surrender their weapons by 27 May at noon, the battalion will carry out a mopping up operation." So, Mr. Kevac, this is a daily combat report that would have come through your department, and it says -- it confirms, doesn't it, that the 3rd Battalion is ordered to take part in a mopping-up operation in the area; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: This is a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object as that's not what the document says, at least not in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "To be made combat ready," which is a different military terminology than being ordered to take part in an operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think "combat ready" preceded the mopping up operation in the text, but let's have a look at it in detail. Perhaps you read it literally, Ms. Edgerton, so that we have no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade was made fully combat ready, as ordered. If the Muslims do not surrender their weapons by 27 May ... at noon [sic], the battalion will carry out a mopping up operation." Now, you said was it the 3rd or which one it was, I can't say for sure because I don't have the exact number. This gives you the exact number, doesn't it, Mr. Kevac? The 3rd was involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right, I've confirmed that one battalion from the 1st Infantry Brigade, it says here, it's a light infantry brigade, of Sipovo. It was involved to block the road between Mrkonjic Grad and Kljuc, and in this report that was confirmed. The battalion was involved in the blockade of part of the area around the municipality of Kljuc, and up until the talks and negotiations with Omer Filipovic and after the negotiations with Omer Filipovic it was not involved in mopping up the area around the territory of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then if -- just hearing that evidence you've just given, I'd like you to have a look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P3923.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can I just have a look at the first page of this document. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to P3923, English page 59 and B/C/S page 77.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now this, Mr. Kevac, is a copy of the 5th Corps and then the 1st Krajina Corps notebook, the duty officer notebook, and I say 5th Corps/1st Krajina Corps because it covers the transitional period. And if you'd just have a look at the entry for 30 May 1992, under the heading: "30th pd," it says: "On 29 May, at 1300 hours, a search of the terrain commenced in the areas of Pudin Han, Velagici, Donji Ramici and Sehici." And then if you go down to the bottom of the page, it talks or it identifies which forces are engaged and there is a heading to that effect. And it talks -- it says that included in those are the Dvor Corps, a battalion from Bosanski Petrovac, two platoons of the engineers' regiment, a military police company, a company from the Manjaca training centre, and from the -- your division a military police company and the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade along with forces of the Kljuc Territorial Defence and a police battalion from the Kljuc public security station. Now, you've just said that after negotiations with Omer Filipovic, this battalion wasn't involved in mopping up the area around the territory of Kljuc, but your corps's own duty notebook confirms that it was. You're contradicted by the contemporaneous document; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I've already given you an answer for that day - that is to say, the 27th of May - that the units of the 3rd Battalion or the 1st Sipovo Brigade were not searching the area. Rather, they were in a state of readiness to proceed to that mission. After the surrender that was declared by Omer Filipovic, a number of members of the Territorial Defence abided by his order and voluntarily surrendered their weapons. However, a number of members of the Territorial Defence did not do that. According to the information that the public security station of Kljuc had about the composition of the population and everything else that exists in that area, it could be seen that all of those who had weapons did not go out and surrender their weapons. Therefore, the decision was taken to search the area and search for weapons and armed persons that would constitute a potential danger for the Serb population and the units of the Army of Republika Srpska in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the 3rd Battalion took part in that mopping up operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd Battalion from the 1st Sipovo Light Brigade or rather the 1st Sipovo Brigade was involved as part of the forces of the 30th Division in the realisation of that task. I don't know exactly how many days later it became part of the 17th Kljuc Light Infantry Brigade and continued carrying out their tasks within the 17th Light Kljuc Brigade and it remained within that brigade up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you know, don't you, that, as a result of the shelling of Pudin Han, people - civilians - were killed? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I did not have that information that in the shelling there were victims. I was not in the area, and I could not receive such a report or read such a report from the units that submitted their reports to the division command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, you must know because Marko Adamovic, the man who was the 17th Battalion's deputy commander for morale and legal affairs, and Bosko Lukic were both convicted of crimes related to the attack on Pudin Han and other locations on the 28th of May, 1992. They were convicted on an appeal decision -- as a result of an appeal decision in December 2013. So you know, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I heard that crimes had been committed and that there were victims in that area. As for the area of Pudin Han, casualties after the shelling, that I didn't know about. Then the Velagici school I heard about the victims there, and also that the persons who had perpetrated that crime were arrested, and that the school in Velagici an investigation was carried out and the perpetrators of that crime were arrested. As for --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kevac, Mr. Kevac, if you just focus on the area that I'm talking about, and I was talking about Pudin Han, you could stay here for a lot shorter time instead of repeating your evidence in chief. So just with that I'd like to move on to another area. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I thought that counsel was going to say that he had not answered the question, which he had, at lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes somewhere in the answer you find a response to the questions. That is what happens. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also said today that when you arrived Kljuc on the 13th or 14th of May, you found everything really very calm. Now related to that, I just want to ask you a couple of more questions. It was -- everything was calm -- it's correct, isn't it, that everything was calm because just a week before you got there, units from the JNA 9th Corps, units from the 5th Corps, including a battalion from the 6th Partisan Brigade, and the 3rd Battalion that we've been talking about had executed a partial take-over of authority in Kljuc. That's why everything was calm, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that information, whether or how they took part in the take-over the power in the territory of the municipality of Kljuc. I can confirm that when I was in Kljuc on 14th, 15th of May, 1992, life in Kljuc was normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And life in Kljuc by that point was under Serb control, wasn't it. General Galic, your commander, confirmed that in a military political meeting on the 14th of May, right at the time you got there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm what Colonel Galic said at these meetings because I did not attend and Colonel Galic did not communicate that to me. I can say what I saw personally. And as for the municipality of Kljuc, I know that the Serbian Democratic Party won the election and that the Muslim-Bosniak organisation headed by Omer Filipovic came second in the election. As far as I was informed, he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about anything to do with the elections in 1990. I want to focus on May 1992. So what I really want to do now is turn to something you said in your evidence in-chief this morning, which was that after the warning shots were launched on Pudin Han, no combat activities in Kljuc municipality took place after this. Now, what happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we get a transcript reference for that as has been the practice in this courtroom since day one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you happen to have a page and line number?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll find one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I find --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And hopefully it doesn't count against my time to find one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No [Overlapping speakers]. Mr. Ivetic, I take it that you also have the WordWheel option, so if one word is mentioned then it usually takes less time to find it yourself rather than to -- it's mainly if we're talking about documents that are not searchable as the transcript is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, what was happening in Kljuc after those warning shots were fired on Pudin Han was that there were widespread search operations going on and there were widespread arrests of huge numbers of non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: After the surrender of the unlawful Muslim Territorial Defence in the territory of Kljuc municipality, the police at the public security centre in Kljuc was in charge of their apprehension and bringing in. If it was established that a person was in possession of weapons, they were incarcerated, and those who didn't have weapons and who were not involved in the establishment of the Territorial Defence were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you answer my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic page 47, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question. Were their widespread arrests of huge numbers of non-Serbs across the municipality, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: As far as I know there was no widespread arrest of non-Serbs. Only those who were in possession of weapons were arrested and those who still had weapons even after having been invited to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you, in your position as an OPS officer, you would have known if suddenly as a consequence of military operations, your units were receiving large numbers of prisoners. You would have known; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: People were arrested during combat, but if there had been, units would have reported on that. In this particular case, we're talking about a police/military activity, to scour the terrain and to confiscate weapons from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you again. Carefully listen to the questions and answer those. The question was whether if your units were receiving large numbers of prisoners, whether you would have known about that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such cases, the units would have had to report on any of the prisoners they had taken during combat, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, therefore, would you have known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just say this: In that area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not going -- the question was at an abstract level. You would have known because reports would have had to be sent to you on such events. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would have known about droves of people surrendering to your military in these operations; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we get a reference for "droves".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied because it's part of a question. There's no reference for it. It's what Ms. Edgerton puts to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it based upon a document she has on the screen which says something different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. The objection is denied and the request for clarification is denied. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ivetic [sic], you would have known as the OPS officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you are confusing Defence counsel with the witness which --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I'll just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was you would have known about droves of people surrendering to your military in these operations; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Whatever was received from units by the operative centre of the division was communicated to me. I don't remember that any of the division units included in the report that people had been apprehended or brought in and that they were Muslims. So I cannot say that I had information about any number, smaller or bigger for that matter, of Muslims who had been taken prisoners in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So could we have a look at a document then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 31828.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this, Mr. Kevac, is a daily combat report from the command of the 1st Infantry Brigade at the Sipovo command post to your division, the 30th Infantry Division, on the 30th of May, 1992. That would have come through you, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: That report arrived in the command of the 30th Division and then they would have been received from the brigade command. In other words, this report was delivered to the command of the 30th Division, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: You said that this report was sent through me. I did not participate in the drafting of this report. This report was submitted to the division command where I must have read it. I can't remember. But I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So if you go over to page 2 in this document in both languages, halfway through the page, and it's, I think, the second-to-last subparagraph of bullet point 2, it says: "In the Velagica Kula-Pudin Han area, the 3rd Battalion is conducting mopping up of Green Berets, who are surrendering in droves. Some of the Green Berets have fled and are in hiding. One of our soldiers was killed." Now, you said at page 72, just a few seconds ago, that you didn't remember that any of the division units included in the report that people had been apprehended or brought in and that they were Muslims and that you couldn't say that you had information about any number, smaller or bigger for that matter, of Muslims who had been taken prisoners in the area. So do you remember now, Mr. Kevac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Under 3 of this report, it reads: "Some members of the Green Berets did surrender. Some went into hiding." All the persons who surrendered in that area where the mopping-up operation was ongoing were taken over by the civilian police, and they took them to the police station in Kljuc where they were interrogated. As far as I know, not a single prisoner, not a single individual remained under the jurisdiction of the battalion command or the units that were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac what you can do, with respect, is if you want to make these point, make them in your redirect examination and focus on my questions because I'm sure you want to make your time with me as short as possible. So it's time for a break now, but maybe keep that in the back of your mind, would be my respectful advice, when we resume. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With your leave, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I believe counsel is badgering the witness right now. When he has answered her question in his answer; specifically, at line number 10. As far as I know, he can only go based upon what he knows. The fact that counsel wants him to know things he doesn't know is not a reason for her to badger him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I do agree with you that sometimes in long answers you find something that is related to the question, but often it moves away from it. And, Witness, you are urged to focus on the question in your answers. Sometimes you say, yes, and that answers the question. I'm not going to analyse with you the whole of your testimony this morning, but please focus your answers directly and primarily on the questions that are put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, in this instance he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- because it's precisely that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question put to the witness was not whether he knew anything. The question was do you remember now? And the answer should have been yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And she directed him to a particular point that he is referring and he is saying still I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not these type of discussions, and no interruptions, please, Mr. Ivetic. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'd like to avoid that we get debates and disputes repeatedly which may sometimes disturb the course of the examination. I therefore would like to ask you to -- to well think about any interruptions you make. If I look back at this morning, I saw that -- I still do not understand what the interruption about the combat readiness and the engaging in operation was about, because even when re-reading it, I got the impression that Ms. Edgerton read out exactly and referred to what she had read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: She omitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: She omitted the Muslim forces, Your Honour. She omitted the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not to interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second was, and I'm not going to enter into a new debate, was the page number which again for transcript references of the same day is easy to handle by anyone who knows how to use his computer and you're supposed to know that. [Overlapping speakers].
