utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours yesterday asked me to give a page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have now interrupted me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll consider with my colleagues what action to take. I asked you now three times not to interrupt me. Even if I may not have developed the speed of speech which would not allow someone to interrupt me, I want you to wait until I finished my words. And I'll leave it to my colleagues whether any action should be taken, yes or no, because I'm too much involved myself in this dispute. But I now move to the -- the third, where I think you were a bit early. That was the objection you made based on an assumption, which was not part of the question, that Ms. Edgerton was referring to a word in the document. I later learned that apparently she used that word because she found that in a document which she wished to show to the witness sometime after he had answered that question. You were just too early. And the only thing I asked you in the beginning is to carefully think when making such interruptions and select only those who are really needed and do not unnecessarily interrupt the examination of the witness. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, I apologise if in the heat of the moment I interrupted you. I did not mean to add fuel to the fire and make the situation more volatile. But I must stress that my actions are due to the fact that the Defence is required in cross-examination to perform certain procedures that the Prosecution, at least within this case, is not being asked to do. Instead, the Defence is being asked to expend efforts on their own to find citations to material. It has been the practice in this case since day one for statements where you use a paragraph number to give the page numbers in e-court. I rose and brought that to the attention of the Chamber. It has been the practice in this case when referring to a section of the transcript that cannot be located by opposing counsel to give a reference. Your Honour directed Mr. Lukic to do that today. I assisted him with that. So I feel that my actions in asking for simple common courtesies that are required of the Defence are not attempting to -- to breach the proceedings. Instead, are attempting to make sure that there is a fair environment for both the Prosecution and the Defence where both sides are held to the same standards, and that is why I was rather emotional in addressing the Chamber prior to this break. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies are accepted and apparently your emotions stemmed from one of the three incidents I talked about today. I leave it to that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll now continue your -- hearing your evidence. Ms. Edgerton you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 65 ter number 31828 back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kevac, just before we broke, you looked at this document and you pointed out that as far as you knew --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's at page 73.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- not a single prisoner, not a single individual remained under the jurisdiction of the battalion command or the units that were deployed there. They were taken over by the civilian police. That's what you said? Now, just to be perfectly clear, they were taken over by the civilian police because the army turned them over to the civilian police; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: No. During the scouring of the terrain, the civilian police was present together with the military and there, then, they would take over those who surrendered, they organised their transport to the police station where they were identified and that -- where they would undergo criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, isn't it? People surrendered. They surrendered to the army. The army turned them over to the civilian police; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I answered. I said that it wasn't the case. The military was present and that the civilian police would immediately take over those who had surrendered their weapons and transported them to the police station. They were together in the same place in most of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is when you're conducting an operation together, one of these joint operations you're talking about in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's at paragraph 12 on page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One of these joint operations. It actually -- it actually doesn't matter who's doing what individual tasks because you're conducting the operation together and you have the same objectives; right? That's how an operation works.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: First of all, let me answer your question about operations. I am a professor of operations and this was not a classic operation. It was a forced activity which was carried out after the Muslim armed formations had attacked the JNA column. For an operation to be a proper operation, there has to be a plan, there have to be forces, and tasks given to every of the units involved. In this particular case, this was just a response to the Muslim activity against the JNA column; i.e., against the Serbian police and the JNA soldiers which were withdrawing from the area. In other words, those activities were carried out as a counter-measure after the Muslim forces had attacked the JNA column. The commander of the division personally issued tasks in the field. He was not at the division command, so he was not in a position to draft a plan beforehand. Therefore, the operation didn't have a plan. It evolved in the field according to the situation and the main objective was to disarm the illegal Muslim armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was the objective you, the army, shared with the police forces on the scene; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what the division commander's objective was in those activities because I was not there. However, the objective was to free the area from Muslim formations that would jeopardise the security and safety of the civilian population and the Serbian units in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in doing that, your forces captured more than -- about 900 persons, they were taken over by the civilian police, and then taken into custody; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: When you say "your forces," i.e., my forces, I was not commander. Those were units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let me just -- units of this 3rd Battalion captured around 900 individuals and turned them over to the civilian police; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I don't know that the 3rd Battalion captured 900 persons because in that area, in addition to the 3rd Battalion, other units also scoured the terrain and they were not elements of the 30th Division. You can find this in the previous document that we had on the screen here. I suppose that the total number of captured persons was about that, but I don't know who was it who captured them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I forget, Your Honours, could I tender 65 ter number 31828 as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31828 receives number P7050, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those persons, that total number, were largely Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, talking about the civilian police for a moment and going back to your written evidence at paragraph 12, page 4, you talked about resubordination in -- of police units in different ways, saying that you never saw any order based on which police forces were resubordinated to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I did not see such a document, a document by which police units would have been resubordinated to the command of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, in fact, throughout 1992 that happened and it happened in large numbers, didn't it? Thousands of Bosnian Serb police were put at the disposal of the VRS over the course of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I can't confirm this. I've not seen a document of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, sometimes you can know something even if you haven't seen a document. In operations, you can see how people are operating and how it works, and then even without having seen any document, there may be other indicia which make you see something happening even if you have not seen a document. So you have now repeatedly said you haven't seen a document. Ms. Edgerton is now asking whether what you saw, on the ground, in your experience, was of a kind to consider that there may be or has been a resubordination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I saw in documents that police units act together with the units of the army in certain areas. Acting together means that those were different units, each with their own tasks, but that does not imply their resubordination and putting them under the command responsibility of an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska. They acted together in the area. There were such cases. However, it was only representatives of the police that commanded the police, whereas, on the other hand, the army officers commanded army units there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just -- this strikes me as a little odd. It sounds like you're actually denying JNA principles, and principles that General Mladic held very close, of the importance of a unified command. Is that what you're saying to us?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question in relation to what I'm denying and what I'm not denying. Specifically, as I worked in the area, I saw that units of the police acted together with the units of the army. How things were at the highest level, I cannot say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, you're not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- previously you said that there was the ones were commanded by the one, police by police officers, the others -- army officers by army officers, and you strongly suggested that there was no overarching command over the two. Now in your last answer, you tell us that you don't know. You said: "How things were at the highest level, I cannot say. I don't know." So, therefore, I wonder which of the two is true? Did you know that there was no resubordination or at least a unified command, or whether you don't know whether it was at a higher level where at the lower level commanders may still have exercised their function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my answer was that there was co-ordination between the units of the police and the units of the Army of Republika Srpska. In a certain area at brigade level, these police units that operated in a certain area were not subordinated to the brigade commander, so he could not use them at his own discretion. It was a police officer that was in charge of them. Now, the joint order for our involvement, that was at higher level. That was at the level of the corps and the Main Staff. They defined tasks for the police and for the army that were being carried out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they would also have decided on any temporarily subordination, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this example, that together with a police unit we were involved in a particular area and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you whether that would have been the level on which possibly resubordination or subordination or unified command would have been decided upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand at which level, tactical or operative strategic level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Answer the question for both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On tactical level, it was not possible to carry out resubordination of police units to the commander of the tactical level. The commander of the tactical level is an officer who is division commander or lower than that. As for higher level, how that was organised at the level of the Army of Republika Srpska, I don't know. I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have answered the question for the tactical level. Operative, strategic level, would any resubordination or any unified command have been determined by the higher-up levels, hierarchical levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At operative strategic level, there is the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Police. The Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Police are both part of the government. At the level of the government, decisions were made for activities of police units and army units in carrying out particular tasks. I don't know whether a decision was made by the minister of the police to have a particular unit resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska and one of its units and -- carry out their tasks within that unit. However, it is the minister of police that would be in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's break time I see by the clock, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It, indeed, is break time. Witness, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, but I'd first instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with any other person, whomever it is, about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that's testimony still to be given. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything that I'm supposed to do is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 23rd of January, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
